name: Hair micropigmentation

image.caption: Scar Camouflage- hair loss - scalp micropigmentation - hair tattoo

lead: Scalp micropigmentation (SMP) tattoos tiny dots onto the scalp so it looks like closely shaved hair. People use it to look like they have a buzz cut on a bald scalp, to make a thin crown look denser, or to camouflage hair-transplant and other scars.

Pigment is placed in the superficial skin and matched to the client's existing hair colour, imitating the shadow of cropped hair. The result is visible right away and is described mainly in news and magazine coverage rather than peer-reviewed studies.

paras: It typically takes about three to four sessions of around two hours each. The look is long lasting, and touch-ups are used over time. It is usually worn with a closely cropped or shaved head.
Allergic reaction to the ink is a stated concern, and a poorly placed hairline can look unnatural. Removal requires laser. No peer-reviewed studies were identified.

web.title: Scalp Micropigmentation: A Concealer for Hair and Scalp Deformities (PMC)

angle.text: Men with hair loss get scalp micropigmentation to create the look of a buzz cut, add apparent density to a thin crown, or hide transplant scars. The pigment is visible immediately, and hairline placement determines how natural it looks.

lead: Hair micropigmentation, usually called scalp micropigmentation (SMP) or a hair tattoo, is a non-surgical cosmetic tattoo applied to the scalp. Rows of tiny pigment dots imitate the shadow of closely cut hair, so a bald scalp reads as a clean buzz cut, a thinning crown or part line looks denser, and hair-transplant or other scalp scars blend in.[1][2]

The procedure grew out of permanent makeup. A book chapter by hair-restoration physicians dates the first published use of micropigmentation for scalp scars to 2001 and the first UK clinic marketing a shaved-hair look to 2002, followed by rapid commercial growth, uneven quality, and improved pigments and training in the 2010s and 2020s.[3] Wikipedia describes it as typically three to four sessions of about two hours, with pigment matched to the client's existing hair colour and laser removal available.[1]

Dermatology reviews present SMP as a camouflage option alongside medication and transplantation, particularly where cicatricial alopecia or poor donor supply leaves few other choices.[4][5] A 2015 review from the New Hair Institute reports very high patient satisfaction in its series, while noting there is no formal training programme and describing complications ranging from colour change to infection.[2][6] Professional bodies including the International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery have begun publishing terminology and standards for practitioners.[7]

paras: The technique deposits pigment in the superficial skin in a stippling pattern, using cosmetic tattoo instruments and pigments, to imitate hair follicles.[2] A tattoo instrument with one to six needles places the pigment in the upper dermis, and the operator judges depth by feel and sight.[6] Practitioners may perform a small patch test first for ink allergy, and the hairline is described as the most important part of the work, with a poorly executed hairline looking unnatural. The hairline can reportedly be adjusted or touched up over time.[1]

On trichoscopy, SMP appears as evenly spaced, homogenous grey to black round dots that are larger than adjacent hair follicles, a finding that has been correlated with histopathology in a case report.[8]

The ISHRS terminology paper notes that SMP and tattooing involve the same action of implanting ink into the scalp and that differences are largely about equipment and medium; it distinguishes carbon-based 'inks', described as more UV-resistant, from metallic-oxide 'pigments' that can fade or change colour over time.[7]

Tattooing for permanent makeup is traced to a UK tattoo artist in 1902, and micropigmentation of eyebrows, eyeliner and lips became popular in the 1980s.[3] Earlier scalp tattoos were used to darken the scalp in people with alopecia, but results were described as aesthetically poor.[6]

The 2015 review by William Rassman and colleagues links SMP's emergence to the deformities left by 1950s-1990s hair-transplant methods such as strip harvesting and depleted or scarred donor areas.[6] The later book chapter dates the first published use for scalp scars to 2001 by Avar Traquna, and a clinic founded by Ian Watson in the UK in 2002 as promoting a shaved-hair look.[3] The market expanded quickly until about 2010, and the authors say many early results looked blue, blotchy or solid, often from clinics run by staff without hair-loss training.[3]

Around 2009, Milena Lardi in Milan developed scalp trichopigmentation (STP), a temporary approach using pigments designed to fade completely.[3] In March 2019 the British Association of Hair Restoration Surgery created an affiliate category for SMP practitioners, citing a lack of professional standards.[7] A 2012 ABC News pros-and-cons piece, a 2013 Men's Health explainer and a 2013 Hollywood Reporter article on celebrity options brought it to a wider audience.[1]

A review of the technique lists a range of alopecias that are hard to treat and hair-transplant deformities as conditions SMP can conceal; the 2015 paper names scars, alopecia areata and totalis, female pattern thinning, donor-area scarring and regional thinning.[2][6] A 2022 review states SMP is now considered a major means of hair-loss management alongside medication and transplantation, and covers the practical principles for natural-looking results.[9] A hair camouflage review includes SMP among options from hairpieces to permanent methods.[4]

Three appearance uses recur: a shaved look for men with advanced pattern baldness or poor donor supply, density in diffuse thinning, and scar camouflage, including as a complement to hair transplant surgery.[3] A 2024 retrospective study of 40 women with female pattern hair loss who had undergone both transplantation and SMP examined factors, including measured hair density and caliber, that might guide choosing between them.[10] A 2021 craniofacial surgery paper presents SMP as a useful procedure in hair restoration.[11]

Key variables named by practitioners and reviewers include pigment type, depth, needle type, the duration and cycles of needle contact, and the timing between sessions; two to four passes are typical and three sessions is described as current market standard.[3] Pigment held only in the epidermis is gradually shed, while dermal pigment persists, and the 2015 review recommends two to four sessions.[6]

Variants include conventional SMP, described as permanent but fading to a lighter grey over two to three years with touch-ups every two to four years, and STP with iron-oxide pigments that fade fully in roughly six to 24 months.[3] Design choices such as hairline height and shape, which can ignore future hair loss when set too low or too straight, are listed as a source of poor outcomes.[3]

Published work is mostly narrative reviews, technique descriptions and small series. The 2015 review reports high patient satisfaction without quantitative data and discusses tattoo-pigment histology and regulation,[2][6] the 2013 review covers technical considerations,[12] and a 2024 comparative study reviewed 40 female patients treated with both transplantation and SMP.[10] No large randomized trials were identified.
A 2022 case report correlated trichoscopic and histologic features of SMP.[8]

The 2015 review lists pigment bleeding, colour change to a blue or green tint on black or grey pigments, touch-up needs, infection including nontuberculous mycobacteria, allergic reactions, granulomas and MRI complications, and says UV exposure can accelerate colour change; it notes that long-term safety of tattoo inks is poorly understood and that many problems are attributed to inexperienced practitioners.[6] The book chapter adds migration that can produce a blotchy 'helmet' look, poor retention with shallow placement, and sunburn as an aftercare issue.[3]

Wikipedia states that allergic reactions are a concern patch testing aims to address, and that no long-term side-effect data have been reported over the past decade with reputable ink, a statement flagged as needing a citation.[1] The 2013 review notes each patient's skin holds the dye differently, so the technique is customised and sometimes needs several sessions.[12] The ISHRS paper cites possible blood-borne disease transmission if incorrect needles or machines are used.[7]

In the US the FDA treats tattoo inks as cosmetics and has traditionally not regulated them, with tattoo practice regulated locally by state.[6] In the UK, BAHRS requires SMP-specific level 4 qualification and blood-borne pathogen training for its practitioner affiliates.[7] For removal, laser treatment is used, and the book chapter estimates modern SMP typically needs one to two visits, while STP can be left to fade.[3]

Coverage of celebrity scalp tattoos appeared in The Hollywood Reporter in 2013, and ABC News and Men's Health ran pros-and-cons pieces in 2012 and 2013 respectively.[1] More recent coverage in hair-loss clinic marketing positions SMP alongside transplants, and appears in the hair-restoration literature as a standard adjunct.[13]

On looksmax.org, a thread comparing SMP with a hair system has one member saying SMP helps mainly for people who always wear a bald look, have gaps after a transplant, or have diffuse thinning, and that hair systems are the better option for typical male pattern baldness; another adds that a skull shape suited to a buzz cut matters.[14] The buzz-cut framing reflects a broader theme in appearance forums that a shaved head with good skull shape and facial structure can read as an attractive outcome of hair loss.
